title: Massive Haemoptysis: Stabilisation, Airway Protection and Specialist Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Massive Haemoptysis: Stabilisation, Airway Protection and Specialist Referral
findings: Built as an additive Disease Management version using the approved-topic structure.
Investigations are ordered from bedside/laboratory assessment to imaging and specialist tests.
The original outline remains current; this version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national massive-haemoptysis pathway was opened.
Tranexamic-acid dose and benefit were not sufficiently source-verified and are not included.

pathophysiology.summary: Bleeding usually arises from hypertrophied systemic bronchial arteries. Airway obstruction and asphyxia can kill before exsanguination. Bronchial artery embolisation can control the culprit arterial supply.
keyMechanisms: Bleeding usually arises from hypertrophied systemic bronchial arteries.
Airway obstruction and asphyxia can kill before exsanguination.
Bronchial artery embolisation can control the culprit arterial supply.

symptoms: Coughing blood, breathlessness, chest discomfort or choking.
physicalSigns: Active airway bleeding, hypoxaemia, tachypnoea, shock or reduced consciousness.
redFlags: Ongoing bleeding with airway compromise, gas-exchange failure or haemodynamic instability.
Bleeding into the only functioning lung or inability to clear secretions.
precipitants: Bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, malignancy, fungal disease, vascular lesion or anticoagulation.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Nausea, gastrointestinal blood and no cough.
Nasal or oropharyngeal source on examination.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Activate anaesthesia, respiratory, critical-care and interventional-radiology teams immediately.
ruleIn.normalValue: Patent airway; oxygenation and blood pressure within age-appropriate range

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise airway and circulation
actions: Position bleeding side down when known; give oxygen and suction; summon expert airway help.
Use a large-bore endotracheal tube if intubation is required and activate major-haemorrhage support for shock.

clinicalManagement.title: Localise and control bleeding
actions: Obtain computed tomography angiography when feasible and refer immediately for bronchial artery embolisation.
Use bronchoscopy for airway clearance or localisation within the specialist plan.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate and disposition
actions: Admit to critical care after life-threatening bleeding.
Arrange thoracic surgery when embolisation fails or a surgically correctable lesion requires treatment.

medicationPlan.note: No routine medicine stops life-threatening haemoptysis. Airway control and urgent embolisation are definitive; haemostatic products, anticoagulant reversal and antimicrobials must follow the cause-specific local protocol.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Severity is defined by physiological threat and airway compromise, not volume alone.

teaching.scope: Massive Haemoptysis: Stabilisation, Airway Protection and Specialist Referral
learningObjectives: Recognise the emergency and relevant red flags.
Select the correct investigation and escalation pathway.
Use medicines only within the stated branch and local formulary.
pitfalls: Delaying specialist escalation while waiting for a non-essential test.
Using an unverified medicine dose or applying an adult pathway to a child.
Mistaking publication status for clinical approval.
keyPoints: Ongoing bleeding with airway compromise, gas-exchange failure or haemodynamic instability.
Bleeding into the only functioning lung or inability to clear secretions.
